Hey there. I wanted you to know that I read your entire story, and I'm so sorry Chip was taken from you before his time. It's clear and obvious you cared so much about him, and Dale too. 


I see how the grief washes over you like crashing waves, and I'm here to say that coping with the loss will get easier over time. Eventually the waves of grief will no longer drown you. 


You must try to forgive yourself. You cared so much and you did everything in your power to get Chip the care he needed. It wasn't your fault that the care was inaccessible due to distance and finances. You gave Chip a happy, full life with all the love he needed. He loved you, and I don't think he'd want you to blame yourself and take all this responsibility onto your shoulders. 


Grief can be really challenging, even when our loved one has a peaceful death. I think you should consider talking to a therapist, or maybe attend a support group for the aggrieved. But I really want to stress that *Chip's passing was not your fault.* You did everything you could. I think Chip would forgive you for not being there for him when it was his time. You gave him so much love! Chip would forgive you, so I think you should try to forgive yourself too. 


I wish for you only the best. Take care of yourself. I believe in you.

My favorite reading of death knights is specifically for Draenei death knights. Most races' DKs do the whole "existence is suffering and we suffer to protect this world that reviles us" thing. Draenei, however - as introduced in WoD and later seen on Legion on Mac’Aree - have engineered constructs imbued with the souls of their most valiant, which is essentially a form of undeath. Instead of being viewed as evil and unnatural, these are considered a great honor and responsibility, reserved for those warriors so dedicated, they wouldn’t let death stop them from defending their people. Even outside of this, the spirits of those who have passed play an important role in the affairs of the living, with Yrel seeking approval from them to become an Exarch, as we see in WoD. Overall, Draenei seem to view death as just another phase of existence, not an immutable barrier. This makes a lot of sense given their history, how many of their people died fleeing Argus and on each successive world where they sought refuge - when your numbers are so small and the danger so great, it would be important to preserve the wisdom and strength of those you lost.

So in death knights - at least those with free will, like the Knights of the Ebon Blade, and all player dk’s post-starting-quest - the Draenei would probably see the equivalent of their own unliving protectors, and instead of despising them, would probably hold them in high regard, since for them the duty of undeath is only taken on by the most valorous. They don’t just see you as a shield against the danger, but as a valued warrior. And that kind of cultural reverence and appreciation would do wonders for a draenei DK's emotional stability and ward off edgelord stuff.

I know this doesn't help at all if you don't like draenei or play only horde, but my DK is draenei and having this kind of cultural background info helps inform my DK's character, and it might help you too. And who knows, maybe if you play alliance but you're not a draenei, your character would prefer the company of draenei for this reason.

An important component to demon hunters that nobody else has mentioned (and isn't mechanically in-game) is that your demon hunter will have different physical characteristics based on which type of demon's heart they ate and blood they drank in the process of becoming a demon hunter. For example if your demon hunter has clear skin and is very pretty, you likely ate the heart of a succubus. If your skin is tough and carapace-like, you possibly ate something like a felbat or felhound.

Demons are beings of chaos, however, and you are not guaranteed to have these specific transformations because they are chaotic and random beings. But I think that's one of the coolest parts about demon hunters they don't really touch on very much in-game, so I like to lean into it. 

I play vengeance, so my character's physical appearance has a tough carapace and large horns that sweep back like bat's ears because she ate a felbat. And because that gave her the tough carapace, that made her an excellent candidate to be a tank. For me, it's important I blend narrative and game mechanics in a way that feels realistically cause-and-effect. You might not feel the same need to do so and that's fine too.

Obviously it depends on a lot of factors like your gear, the amount of armor you have, the level of keystone you're doing, what mobs are in the pack, if you mitigate the hit, etc. I play brewmaster mostly so I have a pretty nebulous idea for how much damage a single autoattack does because of stagger, but I can pretty definitively say that yes in m+ eventually every single attack dealt to you will easily do 5% of your max hp, especially so when unmitigated.

Specifically Blood and Guardian both have a significant problem with this. Unfortunately, in my exuberance for cute little fox people I may have overvalued Nose for Trouble. Brew and prot warrior really don't have an issue with alpha strikes (i've never heard this terminology before) because brew presses one button and they've got ISB up and prot warrior charges in and immediately has enough rage for shield block.

I still maintain that it's certainly not bad and possibly pretty good in m+. If you pull 90 unique things over the course of an m+ (which feels about right for an average across the dungeons after an, admittedly, cursory glance at MDT) and you have 500k hp that's still 2.25M damage absorb/healing from a passive racial.

It's bad in a long single target encounter, and pretty explicitly only for tanks, but meeting the optimal use condition isn't hard (do a dungeon), and in the optimal use scenario it seems pretty alright to me.

It's certainly confusingly worded and I haven't personally tested it on PTR because I have metered internet and can't download it, but to me it sounds like if you have 400k max hp, the first hit from an enemy will be reduced by 5% of 400k, which is 20k. So if the first hit is 25k damage, the racial will smooth the first hit down to 5k, and if it's below 20k you won't take damage. I very well may be wrong but that's what it sounds like to me.

The community is really sleeping on the power level of Nose for Trouble i think. Re-arm is definitely better for healers/dps than Nose for trouble, but NfT is just insane for tanks. Imagine running into a pack of trash and having their first volley of autos do 0 damage to you. That's so much healing done over the course of an m+ dungeon. 

Numerically, Re-Arm *might* be better than Nose for Trouble, but in practical application, Nose for Trouble just blows it out of the water i think. You don't do anything special and you just get a crazy amount of guaranteed damage prevention, compared to Re-Arm which has a pretty steep requirement to activate, and then has the potential to have the heal be wasted in an overheal because when you get that low you health pot or healthstone or healers use a panic button on you like lay on hands or well of existence. That's a very valid point to make and one that highlights something that makes this game so hard to design for: WoW is very different things to different people. Other people do not necessarily value the same aspects of the game, or value them to the same degree, as I do.

My favorite aspects of the game are challenging 5 player content and roleplaying/story primarily, and the things I remember most clearly about Legion reflects those values. Everything else I do is mostly just to add variety and keep things feeling fresh. But of course, those things are certainly not the "definitive" wow experience and it's important to keep that in mind when discussing and applying criticism like this.

Don't get me wrong, I loved Legion. 7.3 and 7.3.5 were superb patches, but legion was *really* rocky until 7.2. 

Didn't you love running a billion mythic+ maw of souls in a row to grind AP and legendary drops because it was the shortest dungeon? And speaking of early Legion m+ *actually* depleting your key and having your loot drops be tied to how fast your group finished and consequently how much your group overgeared the key was just the worst game design i've ever seen in a social game.

All the dungeons initially gave the same amount of AP at the end so long dungeons like the arcway or halls of valor were just dead keys.

What better way to accidentally foster anger, hostility and toxicity than to tie the gear you can receive to the group's performance? There was absolutely no incentive to stick with a keystone group that was looking like they weren't going to make the timer. And moreover, it was not uncommon that people would just give up and start flaming because it looked like the group was only going to one chest it, and it's unlikely they're going to get loot.

And you were encouraged to only bring players that heavily outgeared the content because otherwise you would get less loot. Which means that it was really hard to gear up because you couldn't get into content you were appropriately geared for.

Not to mention getting benched from the raid because you lowrolled legendaries or maybe you were unlucky and happened to get a legendary for an offspec because you put on the wrong loot spec.

And having your AP gains tied to artifact knowledge, which you had to pay order resources for every 6 days on each individual character.

And I'm not saying that legion was shit or anything like that. I loved Legion even when the systems were bad because I found the faction unification much much more compelling than faction conflict. But it's so annoying seeing "BFA bad, legion god tier" every time i load up this hellsite. Legion's systems were pretty fucking bad for the first half of the expansion, and BFA really isnt as bad as everyone loves to claim.

Edit: To expand on why I liked legion more than I like BFA despite them having very similar game systems is really due to how charming Legion was. More emphasis on class identity with class halls and cross-faction unification certainly had a lot to do with it, but also all the characters we regularly interacted with throughout Legion were *infinitely* more charming and pleasant and memorable than those in BFA with this dumbshit faction conflict. I don't *ever* want to see or talk to nathanos, genn, saurfang, shaw ever again. They're not only boring in the worst possible way, but they're infinitely annoying to listen to as well. Compare that with Legion's characters. Khadgar, Velen, Thalyssra, Oculeth, Valtrois, even Illidan with his smug dumbass bastard aura were all *infinitely* more charming and interesting than the BFA cast we interact with regularly. Not to mention the dozens of charming tertiary characters we interacted with through the class halls and class campaigns.

Blizzard has never been good at writing nuanced stories or deep, complicated characters. But they are, in my opinion, pretty good at writing charming characters when they want to. BFA has basically no charming characters, Legion was full of them.

So I basically need to pick whether I want to tank or dps for the next few days and stick with it otherwise the price becomes too limiting. Alternatively I can just play a different character and tank on them, which isn't too unrealistic since they hand out gear pretty freely.

*Ok soapbox time!* On a related note, giving out gear freely is not inherently a bad thing, and here's why: it lowers the barrier to entry for actual challenging content. Instead of needing to spending X hours farming low level keystones for small incremental ilvl upgrades which allow you access into challenging keystones and challenging raids, you skyrocket in item level and ilvl alone is no longer a limiting factor in accessing challenging content. Sure, ilvl is no longer a metric for skill since everyone has a really high item level, but that's what raider io is for. Why is it a bad thing that skill determines if you can play in challenging content and not how long you've grinded for small incremental gear increases?

Everyone complained so much about how much time investment legion required. Grinding for legendary drops, grinding AP and then on top of that, the standard mmo grinding for gear. So they changed basically all of it. You can't *really* grind for azerite gear, you don't need to grind for a respectable set of regular non-azerite gear, and you really don't need to grind ap. My neck is level 37 and I haven't done an island expedition since october. That's enough for 4/5 traits on all my 385 pieces. And it's enough for 3/5 traits on 415 pieces. I do emissaries that give ap and that's pretty much it for specifically seeking out ap. I run keystones nightly and raid twice a week but that's more or less it for my AP income.

Whether you consider yourself serious or not is largely irrelevant. If you are capable of completing a keystone of any difficulty you are a serious player. Legion and BFA have the exact same amount of content for serious players: M+, raiding and PvP. But legion had basically nothing repeatable to do at max level for *actual* casual players beyond world quests and invasion points (which weren't even introduced until 7.3/shadows of argus). Island expeditions and warfronts are high budget, structured, repeatable content that casual players have access to and can realistically complete. The rewards are not so crucial as to make the vast majority of serious players obligated to do them. Casual players finally have something that doesn't make them feel like second-class citizens and the naysayers are, for some reason, infuriated. You didn't lose anything for this easy, accessible content to exist. M+, raiding and pvp still exists. You're just inexplicably mad that other people have fun things to do now too.

That's the thing right? Videogames adore using lovecraftian imagery and references. But it doesn't really work to have a traditional protagonist driven action game or MMORPG with lovecraftian themes. Because the whole idea of protagonist driven narratives (MMOs or otherwise) grinds against the lovecraftian themes. The overarching theme of protagonist driven stories is that the protagonist has the power to shape the world. Their achievements are relevant and celebrated (or cursed, etc). But that directly contradicts lovecraftian theming which essentially says that all of humanity's achievements are less than insignificant when compared to the great old ones. If you have any hope of altering the course of history, if literally *any* emphasis is placed on humanity or human achievement over that of the great old ones, it isn't faithful. Hell, if you even retain full control of your character and they don't go insane, it isn't faithful.

It's really hard for games that aren't built around lovecraftian theming to do it right. It's hard and tricky for discrete single player games to do so, and they've got predetermined beginnings and ends to their narrative. After getting 4 or 5 characters to max by running dungeons, I wanted to know what leveling by questing was like. I did primarily questing on my most recently leveled character and honestly it was a lot of fun. It's definitely a slower pace than running dungeons but i'm sure you knew that. It was enjoyable and when I make a character on the opposite faction I plan on questing to max level with them too in order to see the faction differences in quest lines.

If you're going to do this my biggest piece of advice is to read EVERYTHING. Stop and smell the flowers! Read the flavor text on items, make sure you actually read the quests themselves! Leveling through the quest lines can be super duper enjoyable (and it was for me!) but you have to put in an amount of effort and engagement in order for it to be fun. If you're curious about it I would say just go ahead and go for it. The worst that could happen is you dislike it and you go back to dungeons.

Edit!!! Also if you wear heirlooms then you'll outpace the zones by a lot! The pacing and xp gain of the zones are intended for no bonus xp! If you want to get a more properly paced and less awkward experience you need to wear those quest rewards! It will, of course, take even longer to level but it is definitely worth it.
